title: Compute Anatomy & Access Control
subtitle: DBR, Photon, driver/workers, scaling, pools, termination — and who may use compute vs data
mantra: Every knob lives on one layer — and permission to use compute is never permission to use data.
objectives: You can explain what a runtime is, choose between current, LTS and ML DBRs, and know how runtime works on serverless, pipelines and warehouses.
You can explain Photon (vectorized, Catalyst still plans, fallback) and separate it from DBR and GPU.
You can size driver vs workers, compute aggregate cores/RAM and diagnose driver-OOM vs worker bottlenecks.
You can compare autoscaling on classic, serverless, pipelines and SQL warehouses, and pools vs autoscaling.
You can explain termination, auto termination and Auto Stop and what survives them.
You can debug SQL warehouse PERMISSION_DENIED (two gates) and failing pipeline runs (three layers).
You can read a full classic configuration and narrate what happens when you press Start.

blocks.caption: Each setting belongs to ONE layer

blocks.title: Not alternatives on one level
blocks.text: DBR, Photon, driver type, worker type, pool, autoscaling, all-purpose and serverless are **not** alternative choices on the same level. Place each on its layer.

**Runtime in general:** source code is just text. To execute it you need an environment: Python interpreter, JVM, Apache Spark, PySpark, Java/Scala libraries, native and system libraries, configuration and dependency versions.
That environment is the **runtime environment**.

blocks.caption: A plain Python runtime

blocks.label: Think first: the same program moves from Python 3.12 + numpy 2.x to Python 3.8 + numpy 1.20. What can happen?
blocks.text: It may **behave differently or fail**. Code behaviour depends on the runtime it runs in — that's why runtime versions matter.

blocks.title: Recipe vs kitchen
blocks.text: Your code is the recipe; the runtime is the stocked kitchen (tools, ingredients, versions). The same recipe in a different kitchen can turn out differently.

sections.hook: DBR is the software stack loaded on every VM — and its version decides which Spark you get.

blocks.text: In Databricks the packaged runtime is the **Databricks Runtime (DBR)**: the set of core components that run on the compute. **Every DBR version includes Apache Spark.**

    ├── Databricks optimizations
    ├── built-in libraries
    └── Databricks services/integrations

blocks.text: Ryzen 9, 32 GB RAM, 1 TB SSD ≈ **worker node type**. Ubuntu + Python + Java + Spark + libraries ≈ **runtime**. (Not exactly an OS, but a good start.)

**Why versions?** Spark, Python, Scala, Java, Delta support, Databricks APIs, libraries, security fixes and performance optimizations all evolve. DBR 16 and DBR 19 differ in Spark version, APIs, bug fixes, library versions, optimizer behaviour, Python versions and features.

blocks.text: **LTS = Long-Term Support.** For a production chain PostgreSQL → Databricks → bronze → silver → gold → financial reporting you don't want a new runtime / new Spark / new library every few weeks where *something subtly changes*.

blocks.text: **Serverless:** Databricks explicitly says that for serverless Jobs it **auto-upgrades the runtime** and manages runtime version, instance types, memory and processing engines. So *"which DBR for my serverless job?"* is usually the wrong question.

sections.title: Photon: The Vectorized Engine
sections.hook: Same code, same Catalyst plan — a faster C++ engine executes it underneath.

blocks.text: **Photon** is the Databricks-native **vectorized execution engine**.

items: NOT a replacement of Spark as a programming model

blocks.caption: Catalyst still plans — Photon doesn't replace it

blocks.text: **Vectorized:** row-at-a-time loads row 1, calculates, loads row 2… Vectorized processes a whole batch `[100, 200, 300, 400, …]` of `amount * 1.24` at once. CPUs use **SIMD** — *Single Instruction, Multiple Data*. Photon processes batches of **thousands of rows**.
**No code change:** you still write `df.groupBy("country").sum("amount")` — never `photon.groupBy(...)`. Spark API → Catalyst → Photon.

Scan        → Photon
Filter      → Photon
SomeUnsupportedOperation → Spark/JVM (fallback)
Aggregate
blocks.caption: Unsupported operator? Fallback, not failure

blocks.title: Fallback
blocks.text: If Photon doesn't support an operator, the query does NOT fail — that part falls back to Spark/JVM. Photon and regular Spark can participate in the same workload.
The "other option" to Photon is simply **Photon OFF → traditional Spark JVM execution**. There is no third general engine.

sections.title: Photon per Compute, vs GPU, vs Runtime
sections.hook: Where is Photon on by default, and why it is neither a GPU nor a DBR.

blocks.title: Photon ≠ GPU acceleration
blocks.text: Photon = **CPU-native vectorized SQL/DataFrame engine**. GPU = **hardware accelerator** for deep learning, matrix operations, model training. Classic GPU compute does **not** support Photon.
**Runtime vs Photon:** `DBR 18 LTS + Photon ON` coexist. DBR = software environment; Photon = query execution engine inside the execution stack.

Your PySpark
   ↓
DBR environment
├── Catalyst planner
└── execution
    ├── Photon
    └── JVM Spark
blocks.caption: Photon lives INSIDE the runtime's execution layer

blocks.title: Not competitors
blocks.text: DBR and Photon are not competing options — one compute can use DBR 18 LTS **and** Photon.

sections.title: The Driver Node & Driver Type
sections.hook: The driver coordinates — and everything you collect() lands in its RAM.

blocks.text:
DRIVER
                │
      ┌─────────┼─────────┐
      ▼         ▼         ▼
   WORKER    WORKER    WORKER
   executor  executor  executor
blocks.caption: Classic multi-node Spark compute

blocks.text: The **driver** is the coordinator. It holds the **state of attached notebooks**, the **SparkContext**, interprets commands and runs the Spark master/coordinator for the executors.

blocks.caption: What the driver does for display(result)

blocks.text: **Driver type** is not a different software. It's **which cloud VM instance type the driver uses** — e.g. AWS `m5.xlarge`, `m5.2xlarge`, `r5.4xlarge` (names differ per cloud).

distributed rows on workers
   ↓      ↓      ↓
        DRIVER        ← df.collect()
data = 50 GB, driver RAM = 16 GB → driver OOM
blocks.caption: collect() brings EVERYTHING to the driver

blocks.text: Databricks recommends a **larger driver type** when you expect lots of collected data. Other driver-memory stressors: **large plans, too much task metadata, many attached notebook sessions, local Python objects**.

blocks.title: "But I have 640 GB of RAM!"
blocks.text: Driver 8 GB, workers 10 × 64 GB = 640 GB. `huge_df.collect()` crashes the driver with OOM. collect() moves data workers → driver, and the driver has only 8 GB. That's why driver type and worker type are separate axes.

blocks.title: Ask yourself when the driver crashes with OOM
questions: Did I call collect() (or toPandas / similar) on a large result?
How big is the data I'm bringing back vs the driver's RAM?
Is the driver type much smaller than the workers?
Are many notebooks attached / large local Python objects living on the driver?
Do I really need the data on the driver, or can workers finish the job?

sections.hook: Workers do the heavy lifting; the right worker shape depends on the workload's bottleneck.

WORKER 2: partition 3, partition 4

blocks.caption: Workers do the distributed work

blocks.text: On Databricks multi-node classic compute each worker runs a **Spark executor**; docs often use worker/executor almost interchangeably.
**Worker type** = which cloud VM type each worker uses. 4 workers × (8 cores, 32 GB) = **32 worker cores** and **128 GB aggregate worker RAM** — distributed, not one 128 GB machine.

blocks.text: **Driver type and worker type can differ** (e.g. driver 16 cores/64 GB, workers 8 cores/32 GB, or the reverse). By **default the driver type = worker type**.
Spark is designed mainly for distributed **scale-out**, but node sizing still matters enormously.

sections.title: Autoscaling Across Compute Types
sections.hook: Four different things are all called 'autoscaling'.

blocks.text: **Classic autoscaling:** worker type 8 CPU/32 GB, **Min workers = 2, Max workers = 10**. Databricks may go 2 → 4 → 8 → 10 → 6 → 2 with load. The **type** of each worker stays; the **number** changes = **horizontal scaling**.

**Serverless notebooks/jobs:** autoscaling exists but is not a parameter you manage. You submit the workload; Databricks selects, scales, adjusts memory and optimizes. In serverless Jobs, **autoscaling and Photon are automatic**. No `min_workers = 4`, `max_workers = 20`, `worker_type = r5.4xlarge`.

blocks.title: Is autoscaling a classic-only axis?
blocks.text: Conceptually autoscaling exists on BOTH. As a **manual configuration axis** (fixed 8 vs autoscale 2–10) it's mainly classic. On serverless, scaling is inherent — no "Enable autoscaling?" checkbox.

**Serverless Lakeflow pipelines** have **horizontal** (more/fewer workers/executors) **and vertical** autoscaling (larger/smaller machine types). E.g. Databricks may see an OOM and use a larger worker/driver instance in the next update. You don't pick the worker type, but you **can set a Max workers upper bound** for cost/capacity.

**SQL warehouse autoscaling** is about **concurrency**: a Medium warehouse gets more **warehouse clusters** (1 → 2 → 3…) as 10, 50, 100 queries arrive. Serverless warehouses use **Intelligent Workload Management**; you can set min/max cluster counts.

blocks.title: Serverless still scales
blocks.text: "Is there scaling on serverless?" Yes — intrinsic and platform-managed, just not a user-selected fixed/autoscaling axis.

sections.title: All-purpose Is Not Interactive-only
sections.hook: Interactive by design — not by technical restriction.

blocks.text: All-purpose is designed and recommended for **interactive development, ad-hoc analysis, debugging, exploration** — but you **can** use an existing all-purpose classic compute for certain Job tasks. Databricks supports it but explicitly **does not recommend it for production jobs**.

items.title: All-purpose lifecycle
points: start cluster → Nikos runs → thinks 10 min → runs again
Maria attaches → Nikos debugs → more notebooks

blocks.text: **Why not for production jobs?** Developer A, Developer B, Notebook C and a production job share CPU, RAM, executors, shuffle bandwidth. A random `df.crossJoin(other_huge_df).count()` can hurt production ETL.

items: Job-specific tuning doesn't always fit a shared interactive cluster

blocks.text: **Limited exceptions:** iterative development/testing of a Job (avoid repeated startup) and **very short, frequent jobs** where an already-running all-purpose cluster cuts startup latency.

blocks.title: One-liner
blocks.text: **all-purpose = interactive by design, not an interactive-only technical restriction.**

sections.title: Instance Pools
sections.hook: A parking lot of warm VMs, so classic clusters start fast.

blocks.text: Full name: **Instance Pool**. NOT a thread pool, connection pool, data pool or Spark executor pool. It's **a reservoir of already-provisioned cloud VM instances** that classic compute can use quickly.
**Pool settings:** **minimum idle**, **maximum capacity**, **idle instance auto-termination**.

**Lifecycle:** min idle = 3, max capacity = 20 → initially 3 idle VMs. Cluster A needs 2 → gets 2 idle VMs, pool tries to restore min idle. Cluster B needs 5 more → takes from the pool, or the pool requests new cloud machines.
**Preloaded DBR:** a pool can have `Preloaded DBR = 18 LTS`, so idle VMs already have the runtime cached → cluster wants DBR 18 → VM ready → very fast startup.

cluster: min 2, max 10   pool: max capacity 20
now: 2 workers → autoscaler: "I need 4 more"
   pool has idle? → give 4 immediately
   otherwise      → pool → cloud → provision more

POOL        = WHERE machines come from
AUTOSCALING = HOW MANY machines compute wants
blocks.caption: Pools + autoscaling work together

blocks.text: **Pools and serverless:** you don't pick a pool on serverless — prewarming, capacity, machine choice and idle infrastructure are Databricks' problem. Current docs recommend **serverless instead of pools** when the workload supports it.

blocks.title: Cluster takes 4 minutes to start
blocks.text: Query performance is excellent once running, but startup is 4 min. More worker RAM won't fix it. A **pool** reduces VM provisioning/runtime startup latency — or better, if compatible, **serverless** removes the provisioning problem entirely.

**Classic Jobs compute** doesn't wait 30 idle minutes: job starts → compute starts → job completes → compute terminates.

sections.title: SQL Warehouse Access: Two Gates
sections.hook: Permission to use the compute ≠ permission to read the data.

blocks.text:
Gate 1: May Nikos use THIS COMPUTE?  → warehouse ACL
Gate 2: May Nikos read THIS TABLE?   → Unity Catalog
        both open → query possible
blocks.caption: Two separate questions

head: Permission
What it allows
rows: view/monitor (query history, profiles) and run queries
use the warehouse to run queries
blocks.caption: Gate 1 — warehouse ACL (the warehouse is a workspace object)

blocks.title: CAN USE ≠ read all data
blocks.text: Nikos has CAN USE on the warehouse but no SELECT on `prod.finance.payroll` → **permission denied**. CAN USE = you may use this query engine; it does NOT grant every table the engine can reach.
**Gate 2 — Unity Catalog:** e.g. `USE CATALOG` on `prod`, `USE SCHEMA` on `finance`, `SELECT` on `payroll`. **Warehouse ACL + UC permissions = query possible.**

blocks.caption: Gate 2 grants (UC syntax)

blocks.text: **Example:** `analysts` have CAN USE on `analytics-wh` and SELECT on `prod.sales.*` but not `prod.hr.*`. `SELECT * FROM prod.sales.orders` ✅, `SELECT * FROM prod.hr.salary` ❌ — on exactly the same warehouse.
**CAN MONITOR** fits a power user / performance engineer who needs query history, query profiles and warehouse monitoring without changing size, scaling or permissions.

blocks.title: No Standard/Dedicated on warehouses
blocks.text: SQL warehouses don't use the classic Standard/Dedicated selector. They have warehouse ACL + Unity Catalog governance + their own security architecture. "Serverless SQL Warehouse + Dedicated access mode" is not a valid axis.

blocks.title: Ask yourself when a warehouse query gets PERMISSION_DENIED
questions: Can I start/use the warehouse at all (Gate 1: CAN USE or higher)?
Is the error about the warehouse or about a table/schema/catalog?
Do I have USE CATALOG on the catalog?
Do I have USE SCHEMA on the schema?
Do I have SELECT on the table itself?
Am I assuming CAN USE grants data access?

sections.title: Pipeline & Serverless Access: Three Layers
sections.hook: Who may press Start, whose identity runs the pipeline, and what data that identity can touch.

blocks.text:
Layer 1: Can you access/control the PIPELINE OBJECT?
         → pipeline ACL
Layer 2: Under WHOSE IDENTITY does it execute?
         → run-as (user or service principal)
Layer 3: What DATA can that identity access?
         → Unity Catalog privileges
blocks.caption: Pipeline access = 3 layers

blocks.text: **Layer 2 — run-as:** Nikos has CAN RUN and presses **Start**. When the pipeline reads `prod.raw.orders`, it uses the **run-as identity**, e.g. `etl-service-principal` — not necessarily Nikos' permissions.
By default **run-as = the creator**, but it can be changed to another user or a **service principal**. Databricks recommends a **service principal for production**.

Nikos:            CAN RUN pipeline, no SELECT on prod.raw.orders
pipeline-prod-sp: SELECT prod.raw.orders, CREATE TABLE prod.silver
→ Nikos can trigger it (CAN RUN)
→ it executes fine (run-as SP has the data privileges)
blocks.caption: Same pattern as Jobs

blocks.text: **Layer 3 — UC privileges** for the pipeline service principal: `USE CATALOG`, `USE SCHEMA`, `SELECT` on sources, `CREATE TABLE` or `CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW` on the target schema. Grant **only what's needed**.

blocks.caption: Least-privilege grants for the run-as SP

blocks.title: Pipeline permission ≠ output data permission
blocks.text: Maria has CAN VIEW on the pipeline. That is NOT `SELECT` on `prod.gold.revenue` — the output table is a UC object with its own permissions. To open the backing pipeline from a streaming table/materialized view, non-admins may also need **REFRESH** on that object.

**Pipeline compute permissions:** a **serverless pipeline** runs on Databricks-managed compute — no cluster, no `CAN ATTACH TO`, no user-managed sizing/configuration/security. A **classic pipeline** has more infra options, but its compute lifecycle is pipeline-managed (you can't freely pin a Spark version; the pipeline runtime manages it).

**Serverless access management exists** — just not Standard/Dedicated. Built-in workspace objects: **Default Interactive Compute** (serverless notebooks / Databricks Connect) and **Default Automated Compute** (serverless Jobs / Lakeflow pipelines), with **CAN USE / CAN MANAGE**; admins can restrict which users/groups use serverless.

blocks.title: Standard/Dedicated is not universal
blocks.text: It's mainly a classic compute access-mode concept.

blocks.title: Ask yourself when a pipeline update fails although I could start it
questions: Layer 1: do I (still) have CAN RUN / CAN MANAGE — and did the update actually start?
Layer 2: whose identity does the pipeline run as — me, the creator, or a service principal?
Layer 3: does THAT identity have USE CATALOG + USE SCHEMA on sources and target?
Does it have SELECT on every source table?
Does it have CREATE TABLE / CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW on the target schema?
Am I testing with MY permissions instead of the run-as identity's?

Is something keeping it active — a running notebook or a job pointed at it?
Should that scheduled work run on Jobs compute (lifecycle-based termination) instead?
For a SQL warehouse: what is Auto Stop set to (serverless ~10 min, Pro/Classic ~45 min defaults)?
Is a pool keeping minimum idle VMs provisioned?
Could serverless remove idle infrastructure altogether?

steps.do: Check the compute type and its auto-termination setting.
steps.why: All-purpose termination is idle-time based.

steps.do: Look for attached notebooks/jobs keeping it active.
steps.why: Activity resets the idle clock.

steps.do: Move scheduled work to Jobs compute; set auto termination / Auto Stop.
steps.why: Jobs compute terminates when the run ends.

rootCauses: Auto termination off or too long.
debug.fix: Enable auto termination (e.g. 30 min), use Jobs compute for scheduled work, tune warehouse Auto Stop and pool min idle.
debug.mnemonic: IDLE: Is it all-purpose? Did auto-termination get set? Lingering jobs/notebooks? Elsewhere (warehouse Auto Stop, pools)?

debug.title: Workers are struggling — should I upsize the driver?
debug.symptom: Spark UI shows saturated worker CPUs, or massive spill and executor OOMs. Someone proposes a bigger driver.
askYourself: Which layer shows the symptom — driver or workers?
CPU saturated with little spill and healthy memory → is this a worker CPU bottleneck?
Massive spill / executor OOM → is worker memory, partitioning, skew or join strategy the issue?
Would more workers (scale out) or larger workers (scale up) help?
Would Photon or query optimization reduce CPU time?
Is the driver actually doing anything heavy (collect)?

steps.do: Read Spark UI symptoms.
steps.why: Diagnose before resizing.

steps.do: Apply worker-side fixes.
steps.why: The bottleneck is on workers.

rootCauses: Insufficient worker memory / bad partitioning / skew / join choice.
debug.fix: CPU-bound: more/CPU-oriented workers, Photon, query optimization. Spill/OOM: more worker memory, better partitioning, less skew, different join, more/larger workers. Not a bigger driver.

debug.title: My variables/cached data vanished after the cluster restarted
debug.symptom: After auto termination, re-running a cell gives NameError or cached DataFrames are gone; the user fears data loss.
askYourself: Did the compute terminate (auto termination / manual)?
Is the missing thing ephemeral (variables, cache, shuffle, temp files) or persistent (Delta tables, UC metadata, notebooks, jobs)?
Can I recreate the state by re-running cells from persistent data?

steps.do: Confirm termination in the compute event log/state.
steps.why: Termination wipes ephemeral state.

steps.do: Re-run the defining cells.
steps.why: Persistent tables are untouched.

debug.fix: Restart and recreate session state from tables; nothing persistent was lost.

debug.title: A user can't use serverless compute at all
debug.symptom: A user's notebooks or jobs can't use serverless compute while colleagues' can.
askYourself: Is this interactive (notebooks / Databricks Connect) or automated (jobs / pipelines)?
Does the user (or their group) have CAN USE on Default Interactive Compute?
For jobs/pipelines: CAN USE on Default Automated Compute?
Am I looking for a Standard/Dedicated setting that doesn't exist on serverless?

steps.do: Open the permissions of the built-in serverless compute objects.
steps.why: Admins can restrict serverless per user/group.

steps.do: Grant CAN USE to the right group.
steps.why: Restores access.

rootCauses: Missing CAN USE on Default Interactive / Default Automated Compute.
debug.fix: Grant CAN USE on the relevant serverless compute object.

debug.title: Production code changed behaviour after a runtime change
debug.symptom: A production job that ran for months suddenly produces different results or fails after its runtime changed.
askYourself: Did the DBR version (and with it Spark/Python/library versions) change?
Is the job pinned to an LTS runtime?
Is it on serverless, where Databricks upgrades the runtime automatically?
Is the job on a pipeline channel (current/preview) that moved forward?

steps.do: Compare runtime/Spark versions before and after.
steps.why: DBRs differ in Spark version, APIs, libraries, optimizer behaviour.

steps.do: Pin classic production jobs to an LTS DBR.
steps.why: Longer stability horizon.

debug.fix: Use LTS DBR for classic production jobs; test on new runtimes before switching; on serverless use environment versions for application compatibility.

pitfalls.title: Runtime = machine
pitfalls.text: DBR 18 LTS and r5.4xlarge are not versions of the same thing.
pitfalls.fix: Runtime = software; node type = hardware.

pitfalls.title: DBR ML for everything
pitfalls.text: DBR ML adds ML/DL libraries; it's not 'better' for ETL.
pitfalls.fix: Normal DBR for ETL; DBR ML for ML.

pitfalls.title: Pinning DBR on serverless
pitfalls.text: Serverless auto-upgrades its runtime.
pitfalls.fix: Use environment versions; pin DBR only on classic.

pitfalls.title: Photon replaces Catalyst
pitfalls.text: Catalyst still plans; Photon executes supported operators.
pitfalls.fix: Photon = engine below the physical plan.

pitfalls.title: Photon = GPU
pitfalls.text: Photon is a CPU vectorized engine; GPU compute doesn't support Photon.
pitfalls.fix: Engine axis vs hardware axis.

pitfalls.title: DBR vs Photon as competitors
pitfalls.text: They coexist: DBR 18 LTS + Photon ON.
pitfalls.fix: Photon lives inside the runtime's execution layer.

pitfalls.title: Unsupported operator = failure
pitfalls.text: Unsupported operations fall back to Spark/JVM.
pitfalls.fix: Expect mixed Photon + JVM plans.

pitfalls.title: Big workers protect collect()
pitfalls.text: collect() lands on the driver; worker RAM doesn't help.
pitfalls.fix: Avoid collect on big data or size the driver.

pitfalls.title: Bigger driver for worker bottlenecks
pitfalls.text: CPU saturation, spill and executor OOM are worker-side.
pitfalls.fix: Fix workers, partitioning, skew, join, Photon.

pitfalls.title: Autoscaling = serverless
pitfalls.text: Classic autoscales between your min/max.
pitfalls.fix: Separate scaling axis from infrastructure axis.

pitfalls.title: Serverless doesn't scale
pitfalls.text: Scaling is intrinsic and managed.
pitfalls.fix: Pipelines even scale vertically; you may cap max workers.

pitfalls.title: Warehouse scaling = worker scaling
pitfalls.text: Warehouses add clusters for concurrency.
pitfalls.fix: Know which thing each 'autoscaling' changes.

pitfalls.title: All-purpose is interactive-only
pitfalls.text: Jobs can use it; it's discouraged for production.
pitfalls.fix: Interactive by design, not by restriction.

pitfalls.title: Pools = autoscaling
pitfalls.text: Pool = where VMs come from; autoscaling = how many.
pitfalls.fix: Use both together.

pitfalls.title: Pools on serverless
pitfalls.text: Not available; serverless handles prewarming.
pitfalls.fix: Prefer serverless over pools when compatible.

pitfalls.title: Terminate = delete
pitfalls.text: Termination releases VMs, keeps config.
pitfalls.fix: Delete only to remove the configuration.

pitfalls.title: Termination deletes tables
pitfalls.text: Only ephemeral state is lost.
pitfalls.fix: compute lifetime ≠ persistent data lifetime.

pitfalls.title: CAN USE = SELECT everywhere
pitfalls.text: Warehouse ACL is about compute only.
pitfalls.fix: Also grant USE CATALOG, USE SCHEMA, SELECT.

pitfalls.title: Standard/Dedicated on warehouses
pitfalls.text: Not a valid axis for SQL warehouses.
pitfalls.fix: Warehouse ACL + UC governance.

pitfalls.title: CAN RUN means my permissions are used
pitfalls.text: Pipelines execute as the run-as identity.
pitfalls.fix: Grant data privileges to the run-as SP.

pitfalls.title: CAN VIEW pipeline = SELECT on outputs
pitfalls.text: Output tables are UC objects with their own ACL.
pitfalls.fix: Grant UC privileges (and REFRESH if needed).

pitfalls.title: Personal run-as in production
pitfalls.text: Default run-as is the creator.
pitfalls.fix: Use a service principal for production pipelines.

pitfalls.title: Standard/Dedicated is universal
pitfalls.text: Serverless uses Default Interactive/Automated Compute with CAN USE/CAN MANAGE.
pitfalls.fix: Know each compute's access model.

flashcards.q: Classic vs serverless in one line?
flashcards.a: Classic: you configure the infrastructure envelope. Serverless: you specify the workload; Databricks manages it.

exercises.q: Order the layers from TOP (your code) to BOTTOM.
items: Compute nodes (driver + workers, with driver/worker types)
exercises.explain: Each setting lives on one layer. DBR is software under the engine; driver/worker types are VM shapes; classic/serverless is who runs the infrastructure.

exercises.q: DBR, Photon, driver type, pool, autoscaling and serverless are alternative choices on the same level.
exercises.explain: They belong to different layers: engine, runtime, nodes, provisioning, scaling, infrastructure. The UI just shows them side by side.

exercises.q: Which is NOT part of a runtime environment?
options: The rows of your orders table
exercises.explain: A runtime is the software environment the program executes in (interpreter, JVM, Spark, libraries, configs). Your table's rows are data.

exercises.q: Explain what 'runtime' means and why the same program can behave differently in a different runtime.
exercises.model: A runtime environment is everything the code needs to execute: interpreter, JVM, Spark, libraries, native/system libs, configuration and dependency versions. The source is only text; behaviour depends on the versions in the runtime, so moving from Python 3.12/numpy 2.x to Python 3.8/numpy 1.20 can change results or make the code fail.
rubric: Runtime = execution environment (interpreter, libs, config, versions)
Different versions → different behaviour or failure
exercises.explain: Understanding runtime as 'the stocked kitchen' explains why DBR versions and LTS matter.

exercises.q: A program written for Python 3.12 + numpy 2.x is guaranteed to run identically on Python 3.8 + numpy 1.20.
exercises.explain: Different runtime versions can change behaviour or make code fail — the motivation for pinned/LTS runtimes.

exercises.q: What does every Databricks Runtime version include?
exercises.explain: DBR is the set of core components on the compute; all DBR versions include Apache Spark. GPU software is in DBR ML; Photon and pools are separate settings.

exercises.q: DBR 18 LTS and r5.4xlarge are two versions of the same thing.
exercises.explain: DBR = software stack; r5.4xlarge = cloud VM/hardware instance type. Runtime ≠ machine. (Final test Q1.)

exercises.q: Laptop analogy: match the laptop part to its Databricks equivalent.
exercises.explain: Hardware ≈ node type; installed software stack ≈ runtime. Not exactly an OS, but a good starting analogy.

exercises.q: Match each DBR to its Spark version (source snapshot).
exercises.explain: Different DBRs ship different Spark versions — one reason why changing DBR can change behaviour. (14.3 LTS also ships Spark 3.5.0.)

exercises.q: What does **LTS** give a production pipeline?
options: A longer support/stability horizon so things don't subtly change every few weeks
exercises.explain: LTS = Long-Term Support. For PostgreSQL → bronze → silver → gold → financial reporting you want stability; DBR 18 LTS is supported until June 2029 per the source.

exercises.q: Which runtime does Databricks generally advise?
exercises.explain: Dev → current; operational jobs → LTS; ML → DBR ML.

exercises.q: Per the source, until which year is DBR 18 LTS supported?
exercises.explain: June 2029 — that long horizon is why LTS suits production.

exercises.q: Complete.
exercises.text: NODE TYPE = [[hardware|infrastructure|hardware/infrastructure]] configuration, while RUNTIME = [[software]] environment. LTS stands for [[Long-Term Support|long term support]].
exercises.explain: Choosing m5.4xlarge answers 'what machine?'; choosing DBR 18 LTS answers 'what software on it?'.

exercises.q: You should use DBR ML for ordinary ETL because it includes more libraries and is therefore better.
exercises.explain: DBR ML = DBR + ML/DL libraries (PyTorch, transformers, XGBoost, MLflow, GPU components). For ordinary ETL the normal DBR is usually more appropriate.

exercises.q: Match the use case to the usual runtime choice.
exercises.explain: The beginner's runtime decision table. The last row is the most important: on serverless you don't choose a DBR.

exercises.q: A colleague asks: "Which DBR should I pin for my serverless job?" Best answer?
options: Usually the wrong question — Databricks auto-upgrades and manages the runtime on serverless
exercises.explain: For serverless Jobs, Databricks manages runtime version, instance types, memory and processing engines and upgrades automatically. You don't pin DBR like on classic.

exercises.q: Serverless means there is no runtime at all.
exercises.explain: A runtime exists — the user just doesn't choose the exact traditional DBR. Serverless notebooks expose an Environment (environment version + dependencies) on top of a Databricks-managed runtime.

exercises.q: Who decides the runtime?
exercises.explain: Classic → you pick DBR; serverless & warehouses → managed; pipelines → current/preview channels upgraded by Databricks.

exercises.q: Complete the pipeline runtime facts.
exercises.text: Lakeflow pipelines use runtime [[channels]]: [[current]] and [[preview]]. Per the source, current is based on DBR [[17.3]] and preview on DBR [[18]].
exercises.explain: You don't pick 'DBR 18.0' for a pipeline like on an all-purpose cluster; Databricks upgrades the pipeline runtime with a rolling per-region rollout.

exercises.q: What can you configure on a **serverless notebook's** Environment panel?
options: Base environment / environment version and dependencies
exercises.explain: Serverless gives a user-configurable application environment (libraries, dependencies, environment version) on top of a Databricks-managed runtime.

exercises.q: Photon is a vectorized execution engine. Which statement about it is TRUE (the odd one out among the false ones)?
options: Photon executes supported operators natively in C++
exercises.explain: Photon is not a runtime version, VM, database, file format or Spark-replacing programming model. It executes supported physical-plan operators natively in C++ on columnar batches.

exercises.q: When Photon is used, it replaces the Catalyst optimizer.
exercises.explain: Catalyst still plans and optimizes. Photon takes over execution of supported operators. (Final test Q5.)

exercises.q: Order the path of a DataFrame query with Photon ON.
exercises.explain: Photon only enters after the physical plan; it replaces the JVM execution layer for supported operations.

exercises.q: What does SIMD stand for, and why does Photon care?
options: Single Instruction, Multiple Data — process many values per instruction on batches
exercises.explain: Vectorized engines process batches (thousands of rows) and modern CPUs apply one instruction to many values at once.

exercises.q: To use Photon you must rewrite code as `photon.groupBy(...)`.
exercises.explain: No code change: the same DataFrame/SQL code goes Spark API → Catalyst → Photon.

exercises.q: A physical plan contains an operator Photon doesn't support. What happens?
options: That part falls back to Spark/JVM execution
exercises.explain: Photon and regular Spark/JVM execution can participate in the same workload — unsupported operations fall back.

exercises.q: What is the alternative when Photon is OFF or unsupported?
exercises.explain: The main comparison is Spark traditional JVM execution vs Photon native execution. There's no third general engine. (Final test Q4.)

exercises.q: The vectorized example computes `amount * 1.24`. For amount = 300, what's the result?
exercises.explain: 300 × 1.24 = 372. Row-at-a-time loads and computes each row; vectorized applies the multiplication to a whole batch at once.

exercises.q: Photon: always on, or configurable?
exercises.explain: Serverless and warehouses: enabled. Classic all-purpose/jobs/pipelines: toggled via the Photon setting.

exercises.q: Photon = GPU acceleration.
exercises.explain: Photon is a CPU-native vectorized SQL/DataFrame engine. GPU is a hardware accelerator for deep learning/matrix ops/training. Classic GPU compute doesn't even support Photon.

exercises.q: A compute can use DBR 18 LTS and Photon at the same time.
exercises.explain: DBR = software environment; Photon = execution engine inside it. Not competing options. (Final test Q2.)

exercises.q: Match each term to its axis.
exercises.explain: Keeping axes apart prevents 'Photon = GPU' and 'DBR vs Photon' confusions.

exercises.q: Interview: "What is Photon and how does it relate to DBR?"
exercises.model: Photon is Databricks' native C++ vectorized execution engine for supported Spark SQL/DataFrame operations. Catalyst still plans the query; Photon executes supported operators on columnar batches using SIMD, falling back to JVM Spark for unsupported ones. It lives inside the DBR's execution layer — DBR is the software environment, Photon the engine — so a compute can run DBR 18 LTS with Photon on. It needs no code changes and is not GPU acceleration.
exercises.explain: A complete answer separates engine, planner, runtime and hardware.

exercises.q: Which line in this classic compute plan is invalid?
exercises.fix: Photon: Disabled (not supported on classic GPU compute)
exercises.explain: Classic GPU compute doesn't support Photon. Everything else is a sensible DL configuration.

exercises.q: What is the driver's role?
options: Coordinator: holds notebook state & SparkContext, builds plans/tasks, schedules them on workers
exercises.explain: The driver interprets commands, plans, builds stages/tasks, schedules and monitors them, and returns results to the notebook. Workers do the bulk distributed processing.

exercises.q: Driver 8 GB, workers 10 × 64 GB. What's the total **worker** RAM (GB)?
exercises.explain: 10 × 64 = 640 GB — but collect() needs the result to fit in the 8 GB driver, not in 640 GB.

exercises.q: With 20 workers × 64 GB and an 8 GB driver, you can safely `collect()` a 100 GB result.
exercises.explain: collect() gathers the result on the driver, which has 8 GB → driver OOM. (Final test Q8.)

exercises.q: Order what the driver does for `display(result)`.
exercises.explain: Plan → tasks → schedule → monitor → return. The driver coordinates; workers execute.

exercises.q: What is **driver type**?
options: A different Spark software for the driver
The cloud VM instance type used for the driver (e.g. m5.2xlarge)
exercises.explain: Driver type = VM shape of the Spark driver/coordinator. Names differ per cloud. (Final test Q7.)

exercises.q: Which is NOT listed as a driver-memory stressor?
options: Large plans / too much task metadata
Many attached notebook sessions and local Python objects
Many partitions spilled by executors to local disk
exercises.explain: Executor spill is a worker-side issue. Driver stressors: collected data, large plans, task metadata, many sessions, local Python objects.

exercises.q: Driver: 8 GB. Workers: 10 × 64 GB. Which line will most likely crash the driver?
exercises.fix: display(agg)  # or aggregate/write on workers instead of collecting the huge DataFrame
exercises.explain: collect() moves every row from the workers to the 8 GB driver. The aggregation runs distributed and returns a small result.

exercises.q: A junior says: "The driver crashed with OOM on `huge_df.collect()`, but we have 640 GB of RAM!" (driver 8 GB, 10 × 64 GB workers)

steps.prompt: What's the flaw in the reasoning?

options.text: collect() brings data to the driver, which has only 8 GB; worker RAM doesn't help
options.fb: Exactly — driver and worker RAM are different axes.

options.text: The workers must be too small
options.fb: 640 GB of worker RAM is irrelevant to what lands on the driver.
Photon has nothing to do with driver memory for collect().

steps.prompt: If the team truly needs lots of data on the driver, which setting changes?

options.fb: Databricks recommends a larger driver when you expect much collected data.
Scale-out adds worker RAM, not driver RAM.
Pools speed up provisioning, not memory.

exercises.explain: Driver type and worker type are separate parameters for a reason. Avoid collecting big data; if unavoidable, size the driver.

exercises.q: 4 workers, each 8 cores / 32 GB. Total worker CPU cores?
exercises.explain: 4 × 8 = 32 worker cores.

exercises.q: Same cluster: aggregate worker RAM in GB?
exercises.explain: 4 × 32 = 128 GB — distributed across 4 machines, not one 128 GB box.

exercises.q: 4 workers × 32 GB behave like a single 128 GB machine.
exercises.explain: The memory is aggregate but distributed; each executor still has only its own node's RAM.

exercises.q: Which resource is the workload most likely to pressure?
exercises.explain: Different node families give different CPU/RAM/disk/network ratios; there's no best worker type — it's workload-dependent. (A huge shuffle also pressures memory.)

exercises.q: By default, the driver type is the same as the worker type, but they can differ.
exercises.explain: Driver and worker type are two separate classic parameters; default is the same VM shape.

exercises.q: Scale up or scale out?
exercises.explain: Scale up = bigger machines; scale out = more machines. Spark favours scale-out but node sizing still matters.

exercises.q: Spark UI: all workers CPU-saturated, little/no spill, memory OK, huge CPU processing time.

options.fb: Saturated workers with healthy memory = CPU-bound.
Nothing points to the driver.
No spill or shuffle symptoms are described.

steps.prompt: Which option is NOT a good response?

options.fb: Correct to reject — the driver isn't the bottleneck.
That's a valid response, so it's not the 'NOT good' option.
Also valid for CPU-heavy SQL/DataFrame work.

exercises.explain: Match the fix to the layer: worker CPU problems → more/stronger workers, Photon, query optimization — never 'bigger driver' by reflex.

exercises.q: Spark UI shows massive spill to disk and executor OOMs. Which response is LEAST relevant?
options: Better partitioning, less skew, different join
exercises.explain: Spill and executor OOM are worker-side. Driver size isn't necessarily the answer.

exercises.q: Order your reasoning when Spark UI shows a performance problem.
items: Read the symptom in Spark UI (CPU? spill? executor OOM?)
Decide which layer is the bottleneck (driver vs workers)
Pick the fix for that layer (workers/memory/partitioning/Photon/query)
Only upsize the driver if the driver is the bottleneck (e.g. collect)
exercises.explain: Symptom → layer → targeted fix. 'Bigger driver' is a reflex that rarely helps worker bottlenecks.

exercises.q: Classic cluster min 2 / max 10, currently 2 workers. Autoscaler wants 4 more. How many workers after scaling?
exercises.explain: 2 + 4 = 6, within the 2–10 bounds. The worker type stays the same; only the count changes.

exercises.q: Autoscaling means serverless.
exercises.explain: Classic clusters can autoscale between min and max. (Final test Q9.)

exercises.q: Can you set min=2 / max=20 workers on an ordinary **serverless Job**?
options: No — not with the classic cluster model; Databricks manages scaling/resources automatically
exercises.explain: Serverless Jobs have autoscaling and Photon automatically, but no classic min/max worker settings. (Final test Q10.)

exercises.q: Serverless compute has no scaling at all.
exercises.explain: Scaling is intrinsic/platform-managed on serverless — just not a user-selected fixed/autoscaling axis. (Final test Q11.)

exercises.q: Match each autoscaling kind to what it scales.
exercises.explain: Same word, four meanings. Don't mix 'warehouse clusters for concurrency' with 'Spark workers 2–10'.

exercises.q: Serverless Lakeflow pipeline: what can you still set regarding scaling?
options: A Max workers upper bound for cost/capacity
exercises.explain: Databricks does horizontal + vertical autoscaling (e.g. after OOM, a bigger instance next update). You may cap Max workers, but you don't do the full classic worker configuration. (Final test Q22–23.)

exercises.q: Serverless pipelines can scale vertically: after an OOM Databricks may pick a larger worker/driver instance for the next update.
exercises.explain: Vertical autoscaling = larger/smaller machine types, chosen automatically by Databricks.

exercises.q: Complete.
exercises.text: Classic autoscaling is [[horizontal]] scaling: the [[number|count]] of workers changes, the worker [[type]] stays. A SQL warehouse scales the number of warehouse [[clusters]] for concurrency; serverless SQL warehouses use [[Intelligent Workload Management|IWM]].
exercises.explain: Know which thing each 'autoscaling' changes.

exercises.q: All-purpose compute is technically restricted to notebooks.
exercises.explain: It can be used by Jobs in supported cases, but Databricks doesn't recommend it for production jobs. Interactive by design, not by restriction. (Final test Q15.)

exercises.q: Which reasons explain why all-purpose isn't recommended for production jobs? (choose all)
options: It cannot read Unity Catalog tables
exercises.explain: Billing, contention, idle lifecycle and predictability (Final test Q16). Reading UC tables is not the issue.

exercises.q: Is using all-purpose for a job reasonable here?

items.text: Very short, very frequent jobs where startup latency hurts
Production job on the team's shared dev cluster

exercises.explain: Databricks lists limited exceptions: iterative job dev/testing (avoid repeated startup) and very short frequent jobs. Production → jobs compute.

exercises.q: "Isn't all-purpose restricted to interactive mode?" Answer like in an interview.
exercises.model: No. All-purpose is interactive by design — it lives independently of tasks while people attach notebooks, think, rerun and debug — but it's not a technical restriction. Jobs can run on existing all-purpose compute in supported cases. Databricks discourages it for production because of billing, resource contention (a developer's crossJoin can hurt prod ETL), idle lifecycle and unpredictability. Exceptions: iterative job testing and very short frequent jobs where startup latency matters.
rubric: Exceptions: iterative testing, short frequent jobs
exercises.explain: The key phrase is 'interactive by design, not interactive-only'.

exercises.q: Which code line in a developer's notebook is the source's example of something that can hurt a production job sharing the cluster?
exercises.explain: A huge cross join eats shared CPU, RAM, executors and shuffle bandwidth — exactly why shared all-purpose is risky for production.

exercises.q: What is an **instance pool**?
options: A thread pool in the driver
A reservoir of already-provisioned cloud VMs that classic compute can grab quickly
A pool of Spark executors shared across clusters
A connection pool to SQL warehouses
exercises.explain: Pools are about VM provisioning speed. Not thread, connection, data or executor pools. (Final test Q12.)

exercises.q: Pools and autoscaling are the same thing.
exercises.explain: Autoscaling decides HOW MANY nodes the cluster wants; the pool decides WHERE they come from (and provides them faster). (Final test Q13.)

exercises.q: Pool: minimum idle = 3, max capacity = 20. Cluster A takes 2 idle VMs. How many idle VMs remain immediately, before the pool replenishes?
exercises.explain: 3 − 2 = 1. Then the pool tries to restore its minimum idle capacity back to 3.

exercises.q: Order cluster startup WITHOUT a pool.
items: Databricks asks the cloud for VMs
exercises.explain: Every step costs time; pools skip provisioning/boot (and preloaded DBR skips runtime loading).

exercises.q: Match each pool setting/feature to its effect.
pairs: How many warm VMs the pool tries to keep ready
Upper limit on instances in the pool
Releases idle VMs after a while
Runtime already cached on idle VMs
exercises.explain: These are the pool settings Databricks defines; preloaded DBR makes startup very fast.

exercises.q: On serverless you choose an instance pool to speed up startup.
exercises.explain: No pools on serverless — prewarming and capacity are Databricks' problem. Docs recommend serverless instead of pools when supported.

exercises.q: Queries are excellent once the classic cluster is running, but every start takes ~4 minutes and users complain.

options.fb: Startup, not query performance, is the problem.
Query performance is already excellent — RAM isn't it.
Permissions would cause errors, not slow startup.

options.text: An instance pool (ideally with preloaded DBR)
options.fb: Warm VMs + cached runtime = fast launch.
Bigger VMs don't provision faster.
Photon speeds execution, not startup.

steps.prompt: And the even better option if the workload is compatible?

options.fb: You stop managing the provisioning problem at all.
Access mode doesn't affect startup.
A heavier runtime doesn't help startup.

exercises.explain: Slow start ≠ slow queries. Pools (with preloaded DBR) or serverless attack provisioning latency.

exercises.q: Order the 'cluster slow to start' playbook.
items: Is the slowness at startup or during queries?
Is this classic compute provisioning VMs from the cloud each time?
Could a pool with preloaded DBR serve warm VMs?
Is the workload serverless-compatible, so provisioning disappears entirely?
exercises.explain: Separate startup from runtime performance first; then pool, then serverless.

exercises.q: Complete the slogan.
exercises.text: POOL = [[where]] machines come from. AUTOSCALING = how [[many]] machines the compute currently wants.
exercises.explain: Two independent concepts that cooperate: the autoscaler asks, the pool serves (or asks the cloud).

exercises.q: Lost or kept when an all-purpose cluster terminates?
exercises.explain: Compute lifetime ≠ persistent data lifetime. Termination releases VMs and ephemeral state; config, tables, metadata, code and job definitions stay. (Final test Q14.)

exercises.q: Terminating a classic all-purpose compute deletes its configuration.
exercises.explain: Terminate ≠ delete. VMs are released; name, runtime, worker type, autoscaling and settings remain, and you can press Start later.

exercises.q: Match compute to its termination model.
exercises.explain: Similar lifecycle ideas, different product settings.

exercises.q: Typical default Auto Stop for a **Serverless** SQL warehouse (minutes)?
exercises.explain: ~10 min for serverless vs ~45 min for Pro/Classic, with different minimums.

exercises.q: Typical default Auto Stop for a **Pro/Classic** SQL warehouse (minutes)?
exercises.explain: 45 min by default — 4.5× the serverless default, a cost difference worth knowing.

exercises.q: Finance asks why the dev cluster `etl-development` cost money all weekend although nobody worked.

options.text: Is it an all-purpose cluster and is auto termination configured?
options.fb: All-purpose stays up while idle unless auto termination stops it.
Storage isn't what keeps a cluster billing.
Photon doesn't keep a cluster alive.

steps.prompt: Auto termination is OFF. What else could keep it busy even if ON?

options.text: A scheduled job or running notebook attached to it
options.fb: Activity resets the idle timer — e.g. a job wrongly pointed at all-purpose.
Runtime choice doesn't affect idleness.
Permissions don't keep compute alive.

options.text: Enable auto termination (e.g. 30 min) and move scheduled work to Jobs compute
options.fb: Idle-based termination for interactive; lifecycle-based compute for jobs.

options.text: Delete the cluster configuration every Friday
options.fb: Terminate ≠ delete; you'd lose the config for nothing.
Irrelevant to cost from idleness.

exercises.explain: All-purpose = idle-time based termination; jobs compute = lifecycle based. Configure the former, use the latter for scheduled work.

exercises.q: Order all-purpose auto termination.
exercises.explain: Inactivity-based automatic termination is a classic compute configuration.

exercises.q: After the cluster auto-terminated over lunch, Nikos re-runs a cell and gets `NameError: name 'orders_df' is not defined`. He's worried the orders table is gone.

That would be a permission error, not NameError.

options.text: Restart/attach and re-run the cells that define orders_df (re-read the table)
options.fb: Recreate ephemeral state from persistent data.

options.text: Restore the table with time travel
options.fb: Nothing happened to the table.

options.text: Ask an admin to recover the cluster's RAM
options.fb: Ephemeral memory is gone by design.

exercises.explain: What dies with compute: memory, caches, shuffle/temp files, Python state. What survives: tables, UC metadata, notebooks, job definitions.

exercises.q: CAN USE on a SQL warehouse = SELECT on all tables.
exercises.explain: CAN USE is a permission on the compute only. Unity Catalog data privileges are separate. (Final test Q17.)

exercises.q: Match the warehouse ACL level to what it allows.
exercises.explain: Gate 1 levels. None of them grants table data — that's Gate 2 (UC).

options.fb: He could submit the query, so Gate 1 (warehouse) is open.
With CAN USE he can use the warehouse; the denial is about data.

options.text: Neither — the warehouse is too small
options.fb: Size never produces PERMISSION_DENIED.

options.text: USE CATALOG on prod, USE SCHEMA on prod.finance, SELECT on payroll
options.fb: All three are needed for the query.
More warehouse power doesn't grant data.
He also needs USE CATALOG and USE SCHEMA on the parents.

options.text: The data owner / UC admin grants the UC privileges (if appropriate)

options.text: The warehouse owner gives him IS OWNER
options.fb: Ownership of compute doesn't open data.
Warehouses have no Dedicated mode.

exercises.explain: Warehouse ACL + Unity Catalog permissions = query possible. Permission to use compute ≠ permission to use data.

exercises.q: Order the checks for PERMISSION_DENIED on a SQL warehouse query.
items: Gate 1: can I use the warehouse (CAN USE+)?
Is the error about the warehouse or a data object?
exercises.explain: Compute gate first, then the UC path top-down: catalog → schema → table.

exercises.q: Write the Unity Catalog grants so `nikos@company.com` can run `SELECT * FROM prod.finance.payroll` (he already has CAN USE on the warehouse).
exercises.explain: Gate 2 needs all three: USE CATALOG and USE SCHEMA on the parents plus SELECT on the table. No warehouse permission can replace these.

exercises.q: `analysts` have CAN USE on `analytics-wh` and SELECT on `prod.sales.*` only. Which query succeeds?
exercises.explain: Same warehouse, different data permissions: sales ✅, hr ❌.

exercises.q: A performance engineer needs query history, query profiles and warehouse monitoring, but must NOT change size, scaling or permissions. Which level?
exercises.explain: CAN MONITOR allows running queries plus monitoring/query-profile capabilities, without configuration rights.

exercises.q: Which line of this warehouse request is invalid?
exercises.fix: Remove 'Access mode' — use warehouse ACL + Unity Catalog grants instead.
exercises.explain: SQL warehouses don't have the Standard/Dedicated selector; access is warehouse ACL + UC governance. (Final test Q21.)

exercises.q: Serverless SQL Warehouse + Dedicated access mode is a valid combination.
exercises.explain: Not a valid axis — warehouses have their own warehouse ACL + UC security model. (Final test Q21.)

exercises.q: Order the three layers of pipeline access.
items: Pipeline ACL — can you access/control the pipeline object?
Run-as identity — whose identity executes the pipeline?
Unity Catalog privileges — what data can that identity access?
exercises.explain: Object → identity → data. Mnemonic: **ORD** (Object, Run-as, Data).

exercises.q: Match the pipeline ACL level to its capability.
exercises.explain: Layer 1 controls the pipeline object, not the data it reads or writes.

exercises.q: Maria has CAN RUN on a pipeline but no SELECT on its source table. She can still trigger a successful run.
exercises.explain: Yes — if the pipeline's run-as identity has the required source/target privileges. CAN RUN lets her start it; the run-as identity's privileges let it execute. (Final test Q18.)

exercises.q: CAN VIEW on a pipeline = SELECT on its output tables.
exercises.explain: Pipeline object ACL and Unity Catalog data ACL are different. Output tables are UC objects with their own permissions. (Final test Q19.)

exercises.q: Which identity does a production pipeline use to read sources and write targets?
options: The configured run-as principal — usually a service principal
exercises.explain: Updates execute as the run-as identity. Default = creator; Databricks recommends a service principal for production. (Final test Q20.)

exercises.q: You have CAN RUN on `orders_pipeline`. You click Start; the update begins but fails reading `prod.raw.orders` with a permission error. You personally CAN read that table.

steps.prompt: Layer 1 — is the pipeline ACL the problem?

options.text: No — the update started, so CAN RUN works
options.fb: Layer 1 is fine; move on.
CAN RUN is enough to start/stop updates.
Ownership isn't needed to run.

steps.prompt: Layer 2 — what do you check next?

options.fb: The update runs as that identity, not as you — your own SELECT is irrelevant.
You already have it; the pipeline doesn't use it unless it runs as you.
Photon doesn't cause permission errors.

options.text: USE CATALOG / USE SCHEMA / SELECT on the source for the service principal
options.fb: Grant least privilege to the SP on the data path.

options.text: CAN ATTACH TO on the pipeline's cluster
options.fb: No such cluster permission for serverless pipelines; and it's data that's denied.

options.text: CAN MONITOR on a SQL warehouse
options.fb: Unrelated compute.

exercises.explain: Three layers: object ACL, run-as identity, UC privileges of that identity. Debug them in order (ORD).

exercises.q: Order the playbook for 'pipeline runs fail although I can run it'.
items: Did the update actually start (Layer 1 OK)?
Does it have USE CATALOG + USE SCHEMA on sources/target?
Does it have SELECT on every source table?
Does it have CREATE TABLE / CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW on the target schema?
exercises.explain: Object → identity → data, then data top-down: containers, sources, target creation rights.

exercises.q: Write least-privilege grants for `pipeline-prod-sp` to read `prod.raw.orders` and create tables/materialized views in `prod.silver`.
exercises.explain: Layer 3 for the run-as SP: containers (USE CATALOG/SCHEMA), SELECT on sources, CREATE TABLE/MATERIALIZED VIEW on the target schema — and nothing more.

exercises.q: The pipeline SP still can't read `prod.raw.orders`. Which grant is missing/wrong?
lines: GRANT USE CATALOG ON CATALOG prod TO `pipeline-prod-sp`;
GRANT SELECT ON TABLE prod.raw.orders TO `nikos@company.com`;
GRANT USE SCHEMA, CREATE TABLE ON SCHEMA prod.silver TO `pipeline-prod-sp`;
exercises.fix:
GRANT USE SCHEMA ON SCHEMA prod.raw TO `pipeline-prod-sp`;
GRANT SELECT ON TABLE prod.raw.orders TO `pipeline-prod-sp`;
exercises.explain: SELECT was granted to Nikos, not to the run-as identity — and the SP also lacks USE SCHEMA on prod.raw. The pipeline runs as the SP, so grants must target it.

exercises.q: Maria (CAN VIEW on the pipeline, not admin) wants to open the backing pipeline from the `prod.gold.revenue` materialized view and read it. What may she need?
options: SELECT on prod.gold.revenue (plus USE CATALOG/SCHEMA) and possibly REFRESH on that object
CAN USE on Default Automated Compute
exercises.explain: Pipeline ACL ≠ data ACL. Reading needs UC privileges; opening the backing pipeline from a ST/MV may also need REFRESH for non-admins.

exercises.q: On a serverless pipeline, you grant users CAN ATTACH TO on its cluster.
exercises.explain: Serverless pipelines have no user-managed cluster sizing/configuration/security — there's nothing to attach to.

exercises.q: Which statement about **classic pipeline** compute is correct?
options: It's an ordinary all-purpose cluster you can attach notebooks to
You get more infra options, but the pipeline manages the compute lifecycle and runtime (no free Spark version pinning)
It has no infrastructure options at all
exercises.explain: Classic pipelines expose some infrastructure choices, but lifecycle and runtime are pipeline-managed.

exercises.q: Match the serverless access object to what it controls.
pairs: Allowed to use that serverless compute
Manage it, incl. who may use it
exercises.explain: Serverless has access management — just not Standard/Dedicated. Admins can restrict which users/groups use serverless.

exercises.q: A new analyst can't run any notebook on serverless compute, while colleagues can.

options.text: Whether she has CAN USE on Default Interactive Compute

Not a serverless concept.

options.text: Her CAN USE on the SQL warehouse
options.fb: Different compute.

options.fb: It governs serverless Jobs and Lakeflow pipelines.
That's for interactive use.
Object ACL of a pipeline, not serverless compute access.

exercises.explain: Standard/Dedicated is not a universal access axis; serverless uses Default Interactive / Default Automated Compute with CAN USE / CAN MANAGE.

exercises.q: Complete the run-as rules.
exercises.text: By default a pipeline runs as its [[creator]], but run-as can be changed to another user or a [[service principal]]. Databricks recommends a service principal for [[production]].
exercises.explain: Production pipelines shouldn't depend on a person's account and permissions.

exercises.q: Order what happens when you press **Start** on a classic all-purpose cluster.
exercises.explain: Machines first, then software, then Spark processes, then the session your notebook uses.

exercises.q: Read the configuration: match each field to its layer.
exercises.explain: Each parameter has a different place in the architecture.

exercises.q: Order the path of `df.groupBy("country").sum("amount")` after the cluster is up.
exercises.explain: The whole chain: notebook → driver plans with Catalyst → Photon executes tasks on workers over partitions.

exercises.q: In the Spark compute matrix, which is TRUE for **Serverless Notebook**?
options: Photon enabled, scaling managed, no Standard/Dedicated selector
exercises.explain: Serverless notebook: DBR/driver/worker managed, Photon enabled, automatic scaling managed, no pool, access mode not a selector.

exercises.q: Classic pipeline or serverless pipeline?
exercises.explain: Both share pipeline ACL and run-as; they differ on infrastructure control, UC requirement, Hive and scaling.

exercises.q: Which row is ❌ for ALL three SQL warehouse types?
exercises.explain: No warehouse has a DBR selector or Standard/Dedicated. All have Photon, size, concurrent cluster scaling, warehouse ACL, UC data ACL and Auto Stop; IWM is serverless-only, Predictive IO serverless+Pro.

exercises.q: What's the essential difference between classic and serverless? Then place the runtime in the stack.
exercises.model: Classic: you manage/configure the infrastructure envelope (VMs, driver/worker types, scaling, DBR, Photon, pools, termination). Serverless: you specify the workload and Databricks manages the envelope (runtime, Photon, machine types, scaling, provisioning, lifecycle). Stack from the app side: your code → Spark/Photon → Databricks Runtime → driver/workers → VM/CPU/RAM.
rubric: Classic: you configure the infrastructure envelope
Serverless: you specify the workload; Databricks manages
Stack: code → Spark/Photon → DBR → driver/workers → VMs
exercises.explain: Final test Q24–25: serverless collapses the bottom half of the stack.

exercises.q: Order the stack from the application side down to hardware.
exercises.explain: Hardware ↑ runtime ↑ execution engine/Spark ↑ your application — the same stack read bottom-up. (Final test Q25.)

exercises.q: Serverless collapses most of the bottom half of the stack: managed runtime, Photon, machine types, scaling, provisioning and lifecycle.
exercises.explain: That collapse is exactly the value of serverless.

The Spark version on the worker
exercises.explain: Worker type = which cloud VM type each worker uses. On multi-node classic compute each worker runs a Spark executor. (Final test Q6.)

Its VM shape is the worker type

exercises.q: Which one is NOT a kind of pool the Databricks 'Pool' setting refers to?

exercises.q: Three of these are Gate-2 (data) privileges. Which is the odd one out?

Is a notebook or job keeping it active?
Should scheduled work move to Jobs compute?
Check warehouse Auto Stop / pool idle VMs elsewhere
